title: Gradient Descent I - Intuition and Mathematics
abstract:
The optimisation algorithm behind almost all of modern machine learning. When the
closed-form OLS solution fails in high dimensions, gradient descent finds the
minimum of a differentiable loss by repeatedly stepping downhill. This document
covers the intuition, the update rule and every symbol in it, the full derivation
of the gradients for linear regression, why the learning rate is the critical
hyperparameter, the convergence conditions, why feature scaling is a
gradient-descent necessity, and the stopping criteria that decide when you are
done.

blocks.t: Why It Exists
From the notes

items: In higher dimensions the OLS method to find $m$ and $c$ fails.
It helps to find the minima of a differentiable function.
Used in many algorithms and in Deep Learning.

Gradient descent is an optimisation algorithm used to minimise
 the loss (error) of a machine learning model.

It adjusts the model parameters step by step to reduce prediction
 error.
The step size is the learning rate $(\eta)$.

head: Reason OLS fails
Detail
Gradient descent
rows: $X^{\!\top}X$ is $p\times p$; at $p=10^5$ that is 80 GB
Fails outright when features are collinear
Logistic regression, SVM and neural networks have none
Needs all the data at once

blocks.t: The hill-descent picture

You are on a foggy hillside and want to reach the valley. You cannot see the
bottom, but you can feel which way is downhill under your feet. So you take a step
in the steepest downhill direction, feel again, and repeat. As the ground flattens
your steps naturally shorten, and when it is level you have arrived.

The gradient is "which way is downhill", and the learning rate is your stride
length.
The Update Rule
From the notes
\boxed{ \text{New value}=\text{Old value}-\text{Step size} (\eta)\times\text{slope} }
and specifically

m_{\text{new}} = m - \eta\times\left(\text{slope w.r.t. } m\right),
 \qquad
 c_{\text{new}} = c - \eta\times\left(\text{slope w.r.t. } c\right).

blocks.cap:
Left: the path taken across the loss surface from a random starting
 point to the minimum. Right: why the algorithm self-regulates — the step is
 proportional to the slope, so it takes large steps when far from the minimum
 and small ones as it approaches.

blocks.t: Why the minus sign

The gradient $\nabla L$ points in the direction of steepest increase. We
want to decrease, so we move in the direction $-\nabla L$. Formally, a first-order
Taylor expansion gives

L(\theta-\eta\nabla L) \approx L(\theta)-\eta\|\nabla L\|^{2}
 \le L(\theta)

for small enough $\eta$, since $\|\nabla L\|^2\ge0$. Each step is
guaranteed to reduce the loss provided $\eta$ is small enough — and the
qualifier is exactly what makes the learning rate matter.
The self-regulating property

Notice that no explicit "slow down near the end" rule is needed. The step is
$\eta\times$slope, and the slope shrinks to zero at the minimum, so the steps
shrink automatically. At the minimum the slope is zero and the parameters stop
moving — which is why "the slope is almost 0" is a stopping condition.
The Gradients, Derived
Setting up
With $\hat y_i = mx_i+c$ and the mean squared error
L(m,c)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i-mx_i-c\right)^{2},
apply the chain rule. Let $e_i=y_i-mx_i-c$.

\boxed{ \frac{\partial L}{\partial m}
 =-\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\left(y_i-mx_i-c\right) }

\boxed{ \frac{\partial L}{\partial c}
 =-\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i-mx_i-c\right) }
In matrix form, for any number of features
With $X$ of shape $n\times p$ (including the intercept column) and weights $w$:

and the update is $w \leftarrow w-\eta\nabla_w L$. This single line is the whole
algorithm, and it generalises to any differentiable loss by substituting a
different $\nabla_w L$.

Sanity check: setting $\nabla_w L=0$ gives $X^{\!\top}(y-Xw)=0$, which is exactly
the normal equations of Topic 36. Gradient descent converges to the OLS solution
— it just gets there iteratively.
The Algorithm
The steps, from the notes

items: Start with random $m$, $c$ — e.g. $m=5$, $c=10$.

Predict the output, $\hat y = mx+c$, and calculate the error
 $=$ actual $-$ predicted.
Find the slope / gradient by differentiating.

See how the loss changes when changing $m$ or $c$, and update
 based on that.

$m_{\text{new}}=m-\eta\times(\text{slope w.r.t.\ }m)$;
 $c_{\text{new}}=c-\eta\times(\text{slope w.r.t.\ }c)$.

Repeat until the error is not reduced any more and the slope is
 almost 0.
Thus we find the best $m$ and $c$.

blocks.t: Initialisation

For linear regression the starting point does not matter — the loss is convex,
so every starting point leads to the same global minimum. For neural networks it
matters a great deal: the loss is non-convex, initialising all weights to zero
makes every neuron compute the same thing, and specialised schemes (Xavier, He)
exist for this reason.
The Learning Rate

blocks.cap:
The same problem under four learning rates. Too small and it crawls;
 too large and it oscillates; larger still and it diverges to infinity.

head: $\eta$
Behaviour
Symptom in the loss curve
rows: Loss falls but is nearly flat after many epochs
Loss increases, then inf or nan

blocks.t: The convergence condition
For a quadratic loss with Hessian $H$, gradient descent converges if and only if
0<\eta<\frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}(H)} ,

where $\lambda_{\max}$ is the largest eigenvalue. For linear regression
$H=\frac2n X^{\!\top}X$, so the safe learning rate is set by the largest
eigenvalue of the data's second-moment matrix.

The speed of convergence is governed by the condition number
$\kappa=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$: the error contracts by a factor of about
$\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}$ per step. A large $\kappa$ — a long, narrow valley
— means slow progress no matter how well $\eta$ is chosen.
Which is why scaling is mandatory

Unscaled features make $\lambda_{\max}$ enormous, so $\eta$ must be tiny to avoid
divergence — and $\kappa$ is enormous, so progress is glacial. Standardising the
features (Topic 13) collapses $\kappa$ towards 1 and turns a long narrow valley
into a round bowl. This is the concrete reason gradient-based algorithms
require feature scaling.

blocks.cap:
Left: loss curves under different learning rates — the first plot to
 make when anything goes wrong. Right: the same data scaled and unscaled. Scaling
 permits a learning rate four orders of magnitude larger, and converges in a

blocks.t: Stopping and Diagnosing

rows: A hard budget. max_iter in sklearn
Stop when $\|\nabla L\|<\varepsilon$ — "the slope is almost 0"
Stop when the loss falls by less than tol
Early stopping: stop when validation loss stops improving. Doubles as regularisation

blocks.t: Read the loss curve before touching anything else

items:
Loss increasing or nan $\Rightarrow$ $\eta$ too large, or features
 unscaled.

Loss flat from the start $\Rightarrow$ $\eta$ far too small, or a bug in
 the gradient.

Loss falls then plateaus high $\Rightarrow$ underfitting; the model lacks
 capacity.

Training loss falls while validation loss rises $\Rightarrow$ overfitting;
 stop early (Topic 40).

blocks.t: Gradient checking

If you implement gradients by hand, verify them numerically:
$\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_j}\approx\frac{L(\theta+\varepsilon e_j)-L(\theta-\varepsilon e_j)}{2\varepsilon}$
with $\varepsilon\approx10^{-5}$. A silently wrong gradient produces a model that
trains and is simply worse — one of the hardest bugs to find without this check.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, n)
y = 2.4 * x + 3 + rng.normal(0, 2, n)          # true m=2.4, c=3

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE ALGORITHM, EXACTLY AS THE NOTES DESCRIBE IT
# =====================================================================
def gradient_descent(x, y, lr=0.01, epochs=1000, m=5.0, c=10.0, verbose=False):
    n = len(x)
    history = []
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # STEP 2: predict, and compute the error
        y_pred = m * x + c
        error  = y - y_pred

        # STEP 3: the gradients, from the derivation
        dm = -(2 / n) * np.sum(x * error)      # dL/dm
        dc = -(2 / n) * np.sum(error)          # dL/dc

        # STEP 5: new = old - lr * slope
        m -= lr * dm
        c -= lr * dc

        loss = np.mean(error ** 2)
        history.append(loss)

        # STEP 6: stop when the slope is almost zero
        if np.hypot(dm, dc) < 1e-7:
            if verbose: print(f"converged at epoch {epoch}")
            break
    return m, c, history

m_gd, c_gd, hist = gradient_descent(x, y, lr=0.01, epochs=5000, verbose=True)
print(f"gradient descent: m {m_gd:.6f}  c {c_gd:.6f}")

ols = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), y)
print(f"OLS closed form : m {ols.coef_[0]:.6f}  c {ols.intercept_:.6f}")
# The SAME answer -- gradient descent just reaches it iteratively.

# =====================================================================
# 2. VERIFY THE GRADIENTS NUMERICALLY -- always do this
# =====================================================================
def loss(m, c):  return np.mean((y - (m*x + c)) ** 2)
def grads(m, c):
    e = y - (m*x + c)
    return -(2/len(x))*np.sum(x*e), -(2/len(x))*np.sum(e)

m0, c0, eps = 1.7, 2.3, 1e-5
an_m, an_c = grads(m0, c0)
nu_m = (loss(m0+eps, c0) - loss(m0-eps, c0)) / (2*eps)
nu_c = (loss(m0, c0+eps) - loss(m0, c0-eps)) / (2*eps)
print(f"\ndL/dm analytic {an_m:.8f}  numeric {nu_m:.8f}  diff {abs(an_m-nu_m):.2e}")
print(f"dL/dc analytic {an_c:.8f}  numeric {nu_c:.8f}  diff {abs(an_c-nu_c):.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. EACH STEP REDUCES THE LOSS -- the Taylor argument, verified
# =====================================================================
m_, c_, lr = 5.0, 10.0, 0.01
print(f"\n{'epoch':>6s} {'m':>9s} {'c':>9s} {'loss':>12s} {'|grad|':>10s}")
for e in range(7):
    gm, gc = grads(m_, c_)
    print(f"{e:6d} {m_:9.4f} {c_:9.4f} {loss(m_,c_):12.4f} {np.hypot(gm,gc):10.4f}")
    m_ -= lr*gm; c_ -= lr*gc
# Note the gradient magnitude SHRINKING -- the steps self-regulate.

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE LEARNING RATE
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'lr':>8s} {'final loss':>14s} {'behaviour'}")
for lr in [0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.026, 0.05]:
    mm, cc, h = gradient_descent(x, y, lr=lr, epochs=400)
    final = h[-1]
    if not np.isfinite(final):        note = "DIVERGED"
    elif final > 100:                 note = "diverging"
    elif h[-1] > h[-2] * 0.999:       note = "converged (or stalled)"
    else:                             note = "still improving -- too slow"
    print(f"{lr:8.4f} {final:14.4f}   {note}")

# THE CONVERGENCE CONDITION: eta < 2 / lambda_max(H)
X = np.c_[x, np.ones(n)]
H = 2 / n * X.T @ X
lmax = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H).max()
print(f"\nlambda_max(H) = {lmax:.4f}  ->  eta must be < {2/lmax:.6f}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE MATRIX FORM -- one line for any number of features
# =====================================================================
def gd_matrix(X, y, lr=0.05, epochs=2000):
    Xb = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]                 # intercept column
    w = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1])
    for _ in range(epochs):
        grad = -(2/len(y)) * Xb.T @ (y - Xb @ w)   # the whole algorithm
        w -= lr * grad
    return w

Xm = rng.normal(0, 1, (400, 5))
ym = Xm @ np.array([2., -1., .5, 3., -2.]) + 7 + rng.normal(0, .5, 400)
w = gd_matrix(Xm, ym)
print(f"\ngradient descent : {w.round(4)}")
print(f"OLS              : "
      f"{np.r_[LinearRegression().fit(Xm, ym).intercept_, LinearRegression().fit(Xm, ym).coef_].round(4)}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. WHY SCALING IS MANDATORY -- the condition number
# =====================================================================
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, 400)
x2 = rng.normal(0, 1, 400) * 1000                  # 1000x larger scale
Xu = np.c_[x1, x2]
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xu)
yy = 2*x1 + 0.003*x2 + rng.normal(0, .3, 400)

for tag, Xd in [("unscaled", Xu), ("scaled", Xs)]:
    Xb = np.c_[np.ones(400), Xd]
    H = 2/400 * Xb.T @ Xb
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H)
    print(f"\n{tag:9s} lambda_max {ev.max():.4e}  lambda_min {ev.min():.4e}")
    print(f"{'':9s} condition number kappa = {ev.max()/ev.min():.3e}")
    print(f"{'':9s} max safe eta = {2/ev.max():.3e}")
    print(f"{'':9s} contraction per step ~ "
          f"{(np.sqrt(ev.max()/ev.min())-1)/(np.sqrt(ev.max()/ev.min())+1):.6f}")
# Unscaled: kappa ~ 1e6, so eta must be ~1e-6 AND each step barely moves.
# Scaled:   kappa ~ 1,   so eta can be ~0.1 and each step makes real progress.

# =====================================================================
# 7. STOPPING CRITERIA
# =====================================================================
def gd_with_stopping(x, y, lr=0.01, max_iter=100_000, tol=1e-9, grad_tol=1e-7):
    m, c, prev = 0.0, 0.0, np.inf
    for it in range(max_iter):
        gm, gc = (lambda e: (-(2/len(x))*np.sum(x*e), -(2/len(x))*np.sum(e)))(
                   y - (m*x + c))
        m -= lr*gm; c -= lr*gc
        cur = np.mean((y - (m*x + c))**2)

        if np.hypot(gm, gc) < grad_tol:  return m, c, it, "gradient ~ 0"
        if abs(prev - cur) < tol:        return m, c, it, "loss stopped improving"
        prev = cur
    return m, c, max_iter, "hit max_iter"

m2, c2, iters, why = gd_with_stopping(x, y)
print(f"\nstopped after {iters} iterations: {why}")
print(f"m {m2:.6f}  c {c2:.6f}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. SKLEARN'S VERSION -- always inside a scaling pipeline
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
sgd = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    SGDRegressor(loss="squared_error", learning_rate="constant",
                                 eta0=0.01, max_iter=5000, tol=1e-6,
                                 random_state=0)).fit(x.reshape(-1,1), y)
print("\nsklearn SGD prediction at x=5:", sgd.predict([[5.0]]).round(4))
print("OLS prediction at x=5        :", ols.predict([[5.0]]).round(4))
Worked Examples
Three steps of gradient descent
Data: $x = [1,2,3]$, $y = [2,4,6]$ (true slope $m^\star = 2$). Loss $L(m) = \frac{1}{n}\sum (y_i - m x_i)^2$, learning rate $\eta = 0.1$, start $m_0 = 0$.
Gradient. $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial m} = -\dfrac{2}{n}\sum x_i (y_i - m x_i)$.
Step 1 in detail. $\sum x_i y_i = 2 + 8 + 18 = 28$ (at $m=0$ the residual is $y$ itself). The gradient is $-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 28 = -18.667$, so $m \leftarrow 0 - 0.1\cdot(-18.667) = 1.8667$.

Observations. The gradient shrinks as $m$ approaches $2$, so the steps shrink automatically. The loss falls by roughly $225\times$ per step here. With $\eta = 1.0$ the first step would jump to $m = 18.67$, and the next gradient would be even larger, so the iterates diverge. That instability is why the learning rate matters.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
In higher dimensions the OLS method fails — $O(p^3)$ cost,
 $p\times p$ memory, and it breaks on collinear data. Gradient descent
 finds the minima of a differentiable function instead.

It is an optimisation algorithm used to minimise the loss of an
 ML model, adjusting the parameters step by step. The
 step size is the learning rate $\eta$.
New value $=$ Old value $-\ \eta\times$ slope.

Gradients for linear regression:
 $\frac{\partial L}{\partial m}=-\frac2n\sum x_i(y_i-mx_i-c)$ and
 $\frac{\partial L}{\partial c}=-\frac2n\sum(y_i-mx_i-c)$; in matrix form
 $\nabla_w L=-\frac2n X^{\!\top}(y-Xw)$.

The steps: random start $\to$ predict and compute error $\to$
 differentiate $\to$ update $m$ and $c$ $\to$ repeat until the error stops
 reducing and the slope is almost 0.

The step is proportional to the slope, so it self-regulates —
 big steps far away, small steps near the minimum, zero at it.

$\eta$ too small $\Rightarrow$ crawls; too large $\Rightarrow$ oscillates
 or diverges. Convergence requires
 $0<\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}(H)$; speed is governed by the condition number.

Feature scaling is a gradient-descent necessity — it collapses
 the condition number and permits a far larger $\eta$.

Setting the gradient to zero recovers the normal equations: gradient
 descent converges to the OLS answer.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why use gradient descent if there is a closed-form solution?

Because the closed form costs $O(p^3)$ and needs a $p\times p$ matrix in memory,
which is impossible past tens of thousands of features. It also fails when
features are collinear, cannot handle streaming data, and does not exist at all
for logistic regression, SVMs or neural networks.
Q. Why is there a minus sign in the update?

The gradient points towards steepest ascent. We want to descend, so we move
against it. A first-order Taylor expansion shows
$L(\theta-\eta\nabla L)\approx L(\theta)-\eta\|\nabla L\|^2$, so each step reduces
the loss provided $\eta$ is small enough.
Q. What happens if the learning rate is too large?

The step overshoots the minimum and lands somewhere with a larger
gradient, so the next step overshoots further. The loss oscillates and then
diverges to inf or nan. The formal condition is
$\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}(H)$.
Q. Why does gradient descent need feature scaling when OLS does not?

OLS solves the system exactly and does not care about conditioning (numerically it
does, but the answer is the same). Gradient descent's speed depends on the
condition number of the Hessian: unscaled features create a long, narrow valley in
which the algorithm zig-zags, and force a tiny learning rate to avoid divergence.
Q. How do you know when to stop?

When the gradient norm falls below a threshold ("the slope is almost 0"), when
the loss stops improving by more than tol, or — best in practice —
when the validation loss stops improving, which also acts as
regularisation.
Q. Your loss becomes nan after a few epochs. What do you check?

Learning rate first — almost always too large. Then whether the features are
scaled. Then the gradient implementation, verified numerically against a finite
difference. Then whether the data contains inf or nan already.
Q. Does the starting point matter?

Not for linear regression — the loss is convex, so every start reaches the same
global minimum. For neural networks it matters greatly: the loss is non-convex,
and initialising all weights identically makes every neuron learn the same thing.
